items.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
items.author: Chris Tsoukaladelis
items.content: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug. As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria: Identify yourself accurately and securely Do only what you say you will do Don’t engage in abusive behavior Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm. Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.” This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important: Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next. Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior. For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked. Do not engage in abusive behavior This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust. We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are: Does the bot respect instructions? Did it respond to direct feedback? We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify. When in Rome, do as the Romans do A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time. Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309. And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again. Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it. Building trust over time Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them. This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone. We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior. Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar. And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

items.title: Monthly Roundup #47: October 2026
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: AI might not yet be eating the physical world. AI is still eating the world of news, and I am finding less and less opportunity to post about other things. My backlog of items grows across most of my secondary topics and I haven’t had time for any side projects. The monthly, no matter what, is sacred. We continue. Table of Contents Home Alone. The Men Have Never Been Okay. Antisocial Media. While I Cannot Condone This. Zero Marginal Product. Good News, Everyone. 100 Good Television Shows. For Your Entertainment. Gamers Gonna Game Game Game Game Game. I Was Promised Flying Self-Driving Cars. Sports Go Sports. Government Working. Jones Act Watch. Variously Effective Altruism. Walk Away. The Lighter Side. Home Alone The story of our time, told once again: Americans are abandoning quite a lot of formerly popular activities, especially hosting at home, as Derek Thompson discussed. Phones and other electronics are in, most things that are not phones are out, with notably rare exceptions. That last line rules everything around us. And we all spend more time at home, which then exploded during Covid and mostly did not recover afterward. Derek does discuss the last two lines later on. You can view exercise classes as an adaptation in four ways: To a lack of other physical activity, to a lack of social activity, to a lack of motivation, and as a wealth effect. Regular people can afford this, and it is a safe way to get things they now lack. Then there are the concerts. This one is what some call a Narrative Violation. We have this collective story about how in the good old days, like the 1960s, people went to all these great cheap concerts, that was part of the good life, and we’ve gotten away from that. But actually they’re making a quiet comeback despite people getting older and all the competition, and also they are great. On the flip side, they are also ‘free’ actions, in that you don’t have to overcome any social barrier. You can buy a ticket. Whereas hosting is, as Derek says, a lot of work to set up, often not fun work. If you’re both working, and children now require vastly more time investment because our society went insane there, who has the time and energy to earn the payoff? Parties also require (and help create and maintain) friends, and creating and maintaining those friends takes even more time. Meanwhile, being alone at home is no longer boring. Being alone at home is great, in the short term. Derek Thompson: Machines in the last half century have accomplished something stranger. They have made other people less necessary to our leisure. Every generation has acquired better ways to entertain itself without leaving the house. The result is a peculiar triumph of modern abundance: We have built a world in which being alone has never been easier, more comfortable, or more fun. And then we wonder why everybody stopped coming over. … Is this what we want? At the risk of invoking Clintonian levels of abstruseness, it depends on what “want” means. Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. There is some coordination failure, but I think this is the wrong central diagnosis. Coordination failure can be overcome, and given the will to do the thing the logistics are far easier today with all our social and communication and logistical tools. The bigger problem is hyperbolic discounting in the face of the new alternatives. In order to get the returns from social activity, you have to invest energy and effort now, and also endure some mild social awkwardness and delay gratification and tolerate some boredom now, and often do things for someone else, in order to build up your friendship and other networks and get into regular habits. I’m also guilty of this trap. I don’t socialize enough. I don’t host enough, and I don’t visit enough. I realize this. But it’s tough. There’s too much to do, both for work and for play. In my case I like to think I have a good excuse, but it is still a mistake. The Men Have Never Been Okay Institute for Family Studies reports at length on America’s demoralized and lost men. Their central presentation is not that young men have, as Senator Hawley put it, ‘no vision for what it is to be a man,’ or that their vision would be bad and captured by toxic influences. It’s that they do have such a positive vision, and it would be good but they despair of living up to it and do not see a path to getting there. We no longer lay out a simple ‘success sequence’ style strategy where you play by the rules and it does not work even for those without problems, and many have problems. The men are culturally told that, by default, they are worthless and unwanted. Or is that the real story? There are some strange sets of beliefs reported. 42% think they are failures and 60% feel they have little control. 72% say who you know is more important than hard work, and 49% saying ‘no matter how hard I work, people like me will never achieve the American dream.’ But 84% say they are at least somewhat ambitious and 81% say they can ‘do just about anything I really set my mind to,’ 75% say their opportunities in life will be greater than their parents, and 82% say they have more potential to succeed than people think. This seems like a lot of very strong framing effects combined with the Revolution of Rising Expectations. The men believe all these things at the same time, in different ways, and you can ‘activate different personas.’ Connections can beat hard work and the deck is stacked against you, but hard work is valid, and if you want it enough and keep your head on straight and resist temptation and despair you can still succeed. But do you want it enough? Can you keep your head on straight and resist temptation and despair? And can you keep searching for an unknown, rather than for a known, so long as the ultimate odds have not changed so much? Another way of looking at this is that if you succeed, there was some way in which you got lucky or did something extraordinary. Something individually atypical is part of every typical success story, even more so than in the past. But if you keep pushing, and try to make your own luck, you will probably eventually get lucky. There are charts and statistics about the usual suspects, like unemployment, depression, disabilities, games, social media, atomization, gambling and pornography. Social media is not like the others, where ‘once a day’ is considered infrequent. Over half of young men feel lonely ‘at least some of the time’ but it is kind of weird not to, isn’t it? The right rate of feeling lonely, like many bad things, is not zero. The report has many other interesting charts. It would be cool to see time lapses. Mostly I came away from this report feeling better rather than worse, if you don’t think AI will upend everything. Ways exist to be found, at least for now. Remember that throughout history, a huge percentage of men failed to have children. It is not a new situation for men to be tested and have to find a way to prove themselves. Broadly my current perspective is the men as a group have never been okay. The difference is that we used to sort of think not being okay was fine. Now we don’t. Antisocial Media Texting more often is associated with higher life satisfaction. Tyler Cowen asks ‘should you text more?’ and my response would be ‘yes, but only insofar as you should have more friends that you want to text.’ Frequency of YouTube and TikTok use was associated with lower life satisfaction, which partly can be explained the same way. Here I bet it runs both ways. There was no association from use of other social technology, which implies other social technology is modestly negative, since it should be positively correlated with friends. YouTube is changing its short-form algorithm to further prioritize original content, and especially to reduce reach of content ‘re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own.’ I mean, yeah, why is that even allowed? Twitter identifies and suspends a Chinese bot farm of ~200,000 accounts engaged in influence operations. This included 200 working to build American opposition to data centers. Those 200 were shown. The other 199,800 were not shown. I wonder what they were up to. While I Cannot Condone This If you don’t want to wrongspeak, you have two strategies. You can suppress thoughts, or you can suppress words. Paola: I’m realizing that my ratio of “thoughts that explicitly enter my consciousness mind” to “thoughts I share out loud” must be absolutely crazy relative to the general population. My sense is that agreeable people basically suppress their thoughts as opposed to just their words and it’s at least slightly weird that I’m doing basically 0 thought suppression and a large amount of word suppression. I was always confused about my levels of agreeableness because I felt like a lot of people saw me as “reasonably agreeable” and people close to me always saw me as “extremely disagreeable” and my self perception was somewhere in the middle. Astrid Wilde: for what it’s worth i am probably top 5% agreeableness and i just say what i think. I think Paola is at least directionally right. On reflection I think I have all four modes in the 2×2: suppressing or not suppressing thoughts and also speech. One strives to be in places one can suppress neither, but it is not always possible. In Western Massachusetts, in the year 2026, there was a lesbian bar still requiring KN-95 masks. They changed Saturday nights to mask optional, and all hell broke loose like it was still 2020: “Just say you’re being complicit in a mass disabling event and get it over with.” “People like you kill disabled people in the name of your own leisure and convenience.” Someone else wished the venue would be firebombed. Annalisa Quinn: The thread grew to 442 comments, some supportive, but many furious. The people running the bar were accused of being ableist — eugenicist, even — for relaxing their signature policy in the face of what commenters consider an ongoing pandemic (Greenfield hasn’t reported any COVID cases in more than two months). And then it got worse, or better, I’m not sure which. Instead of defusing the situation, the apology seemed to make things worse. The bar had erred: it posted an Instagram card without providing alt-text for the visually impaired. This set off a fresh round of accusations of ableism. “This is not an accessible post,” wrote one user. “It indicates the lack of care or interest in Disability intersectionality.” It keeps going from there. On the second mask-optional Saturday the dance floor was empty, the hoped-for unmasked customers never came, and the owner ended the night alone on it, still masked. Zero Marginal Product Fun hypothetical: Kurosai: Do you know how fucked up you have to be to reject a job that lets you sleep for 45 and hour? This is a joke. AllThingsBeginWithNu: This is my job right now. Merlins Bread: In certain parts of Latin America where it’s difficult to fire people, this is what they do. You clock in to the basement each day, sit in the uncomfortable cold with nothing to do, and clock out. No mobile reception, and you can still be fired for reading a novel on the job or refusing to follow safe work instructions. This is obviously a terrible deal if you have better options or important work to do, but otherwise? The consensus strategy, of course, is to sleep. You shift your sleep schedule to be from 6am-2pm, learn to sleep either in the chair or on the floor, and that’s it. If you ban sleeping, this turns into the trying-to-get-you-to-quit scenario of Oidashibeya, where we have run the experiment, and some people quit but others do not, depending on their circumstances. Unfortunately, I briefly checked the subreddit, and most posts there are super lame. Good News, Everyone We have an excellent permitting deal, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (S. 5653), if we can get it over the finish line into law. I don’t have time to properly geek out on all the details, but this is a big deal. Even better would be huge sweeping ‘cut the Gordian knot’ changes, but if you’re going to do incremental stuff this would be pretty great. Back in July we got a report to the president called Science: A New Golden Age. In a better or quieter world I would have looked into this in detail. I am sad I never got to do that, but I need to admit defeat. By all accounts there were a lot of good ideas here. Halloween not only is not the ‘deadliest day for child pedestrians,’ it is the safest by a huge margin, because everyone knows to watch out for child pedestrians that night. Yes, the absolute number of accidents is higher, but that is because normally we don’t let our children go outside and on Halloween everyone goes outside. I confirm, based on both personal experience and what I see in others, that Justin Skycak is correct here: High performers start out with an edge that motivates more work with increasing returns to scale, then work more and harder than everyone else, and end up acquiring a vast array of related skills as they climb the entire associated tech tree. You can see it in various places. In sports, where the top players are better at actual everything, including all the tiny details. In media, where high quality things are just high quality across the board, with no limit. And so on. 100 Good Television Shows A remarkably good list, the product of an industry survey: I don’t agree with every call, or every omission, but I do not have to. As usual with such lists, there are many excellent picks: Excellent picks I can confirm (26): 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 21, 22, 24, 30, 31, 36, 37, 44, 51, 53, 62, 78, 94, 97, 99, 100. Excellent short series I wouldn’t count but can confirm (6): 19, 35, 39, 72, 81, 86 In some cases we are pretending later seasons do not exist because they don’t. True Detective is a weird case, where they’re finally going to make Season 2 soon, and they’re calling it Season 5. Nicolas Cage will star. Picks I am confident are excellent, but which I cannot fully confirm as I have not seen them, or seen enough of them (9): 3, 16, 27, 32, 50, 58, 73, 74, 96. That’s already 41 out of 100. That’s also nine series I am suddenly tempted to watch, that I haven’t, but that I can crack open at any time. Several are because they’re ‘tough watches’ despite greatness. As in, I know Andor is great, but do I actually want to watch Andor? Unclear. I see a number of picks here that aren’t for me, or that I wouldn’t count for being too short, but only a handful where I could plausibly say, in the abstract, bad pick. The next question would be, how many are conspicuously missing? I have 7 Tier 1 TV shows. 5 of the 7 make the list, and the other two are obscure and thus highly forgivable mistake. All the straight dramas on my list make their top 20, including their #1 and #2. I have 40 Tier 2 TV shows, 30 of which are eligible. Here the list does a lot worse, and only has 10 of them. I’d only call maybe 5 of the remaining 20 objective mistakes, rather than differences of opinion. That illustrates how long is the long tail of television. This did remind me that I have to make some updates here. In any case, yes, Matthew Yglesias, there are not only 100 good TV shows but 100+ great TV shows out there, and yes you do need a canon so people can find the great ones. Matthew’s main argument is that if you have a great TV show, and then before it gets cancelled it gets bad, then the whole TV show is now not good, and this happens often enough that there aren’t that many good TV shows. I think this is bollocks whenever you can pretend the later seasons do not exist. If Shogun counts as great now (to use his example), and it does so long as you think it is long enough to count, and they then come out with two more seasons that are mid, then Shogun Season 1 is still great because it did not depend on ‘paying off’ in future seasons. The Diplomat, to use another of his examples, is different, because it is building to and paying off things, so you take some damage if it can’t nail the ending. I agree with Adi that The Altruists looks like borderline slander against Caroline Ellison, setting her up as the mastermind that she very obviously was not. SBF was running this show. I would add that the SBF in the trailer is completely unrecognizable from the SBF of which there is quite a lot of film and documentation, and not only in physical appearance. Christian Lorentzen: The problem with adapting SBF for drama is that, protagonist or antagonist, your main character has to have relatable desires, characteristics or motivations while the real SBF seems pretty alien to a normie audience. Patrick McKenzie: I would assume the thesis of most of the projects is “The main character wants money and power” and that is not an unknown character archetype as either protagonist or antagonist. Character would be extremely intelligent, well-spoken, and quite forward with regards to desires. The way this is played in the Big Short is “X is so comically self-interested and upfront about this fact that I can’t even hate him” (that is close to a quote from another character) and I think there are a variety of opinions one could have re: sincerity of the character. This is part of his charm on other people. Strategic or not? I Was Promised Flying Self-Driving Cars Waymo was already absurdly safer than human drivers, and it keeps getting safer, despite reports that the driving is getting less passive. Waymo: 270M+ miles. 841 fewer injury-causing crashes. Our latest safety data shows the Waymo Driver continues to make roads safer for everyone. Compared to human drivers across 5 territories, it reduced: Injury crashes by 82% Serious injury crashes by 95% Full data [here]. Jeff Dean: The safety data for Waymo gets better and better. Comparison w/ human drivers on rate of crashes with serious injury: Latest data: 270M miles, 20X better Mar 2026: 170M miles, 13X better Before that (forget exactly when): 10X better Elan Bechor: Waymos are really safe (80-95% safer than humans depending on the metric), but they also seem to be getting *safer* over time. This is the worst they’ll ever be. A quick analysis of the police-reported crash rates in three cities from Waymo’s published safety data. What is the optimal rate of accident reduction, versus making trips faster? My guess is around this point you want to take your further wins largely in speed. Tesla is taking more risks than Waymo, such as not pausing in the rain. That pausing does get Waymo some ‘free safety’ that one has to correct for. I endorse it. There’s so much risk that one stupid accident could ruin everything. The Chinese are very much in the driverless car race. David Manheim: I just wondered why other countries weren’t deploying autonomous taxis, then checked. China’s Baidu has ~2000 cars under “Apollo Go” in 6 cities. Waymo has ~4000. I’m pretty unsure who wins scaling globally, given the larger addressable domestic market in China, vs Waymo’s lead. This is presumably not winner-take-all, rather it is a threshold oligopoly. If you can get the necessary efficiencies and safety, you can put on the road however many cars you can manufacture, until the market of all rides is saturated. Then yes you compete, and probably we settle into a 1-4 service world in any given place, with 1 for rural areas and 3+ for big urban centers. Meanwhile, yes, it is slow going but Waymo is steadily expanding. The Waymo debate is happening right now in DC. There is a strange emphasis on ‘countless’ ride share drivers, given DC only has 200 full-time ride share drivers among its residents, and as always calls not to ‘rush’ legislation. Sports Go Sports A classic: Nick Saban’s Five Enemies of Greatness. Worth a periodic read. Here are the salary ranges, also known as the long term viability index if no one adjusts. I don’t much mind the competitive imbalance. That’s not exactly new. What I do mind is the constant player movement. There’s too much to learn and I want to be able to root for coherent teams, and also it would be nice to have the players go to a single actual college, get an education, have friends and an identity and so on. Many such cases. On the one hand, dealing with vouchers is annoying and the cost gets priced into the tickets. On the other hand, it makes travellers feel a lot better, and due to ticket booking via de facto auction airlines are forced to not offer such features unless they are mandatory. The airlines do have some influence on outcomes, especially since the top reclassified cause is ‘unscheduled maintenance.’ My gut says it is better to make the airlines pay, but it seems fine either way. Financial Times: Successful applicants will either have to make a non-refundable donation of $350,000 to Argentina’s Treasury or purchase a zero-coupon government bond worth $800,000. Mike Bird: Weird, surely you’d choose to make the non-refundable $350,000 donation rather than the non-refundable $800,000 donation. It is not quite that simple, but it is close to that simple. You are not allowed to sell the bond for seven years, and if you do the math on comparable tradable bonds it is cheaper to pay the $350,000 while also requiring less money up front. Choice is easy. I get that maybe you need cannabis to be legal because of the alternative but why the hell are we advertising its legality in the subway with public service announcements? Mamdani to ban Central Park’s horse-drawn carriages, one of the famous things to do in New York. I’ve never actually done it, but I feel like I should do it now while I can. Sounds like we will have until June 2028. You know it is deeply stupid when they are laying off 200 people and destroying a cultural touchstone purportedly in large part because of one accidental death, of Romanch Mahajan, and also because people think it is inhumane to the horses to have them draw carriages, and various other things that are not true. Yes, America still massively subsidizes shipbuilding, but so does everyone else. If you want to build ships domestically, for strategic reasons, you are going to have to subsidize that. I don’t love doing that, but I also don’t mind it at all. Sure, we can afford it. The key is to do that with money, not with a ban on other ships. Variously Effective Altruism The bad guys have come with bad faith attacks against Effective Altruism, as has the Department of War, and the neutral guys are suddenly paying attention and creating profiles that often miss the mark, as per the usual Gell-Mann experience. I certainly have my critiques of Effective Altruism. Most famously I have my Book Review of Going Infinite. I had Altruism is Incomplete back in 2017. In 2022 I entered a criticism of the EA Criticism Contest into the contest itself, including my 21 points that attempt to summarize the EA framework, of which I strongly disagreed (and still do disagree) with 13, in order to argue that they want critiques but only within their frames. I won an honorable mention. At one point they paid me to come to EAG Boston and give a presentation about my disagreements with EA, which is exactly what I did. And so on. That’s because the EAs are trying hard enough to be worthy of critique. So critiques they shall have, good ones, that hold them to the standards they aspire to fulfill. This wave is different. This is a deliberate campaign of attack, the true face of politics. No one involved is trying to make anyone better. That’s not cool. No one picks on my little brother but me, especially in bad faith. There are plenty of public and acknowledged connections between various EA orgs and people and funders, which causes some to then try and force QAnon styles of connections, such as ‘person [P] who funded or invested in [X] also funded [Y], therefore [X] funded [Y].’ Which of course is not how it works. It’s fun to now continuously see claims of the class ‘Asterisk is funded by Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy). It really is remarkable that @NYMag didn’t disclose the ties that one of its co-authors on the piece has’ when the piece does actually disclose this as the lede of the article. Welcome to Politics, capital P. A lot of the time, the true argument is of the form ‘there are these weird (and other attributes you or your politics will dislike) people who care about AI safety, but as I’ve shown such people are weird and bad, therefore you shouldn’t care about AI safety.’ Then there are those who accuse the EAs of saying ‘only they can be trusted with AGI’ or that they want to take over the world. Some form of this is narrowly true of the leaders and many employees of the major labs, which includes many EAs at Anthropic, but the same is true of many at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and also Elon Musk, which mostly are not EAs. The active ingredient lies elsewhere. There is also, yes, a faction that says ‘no one can be trusted, but someone is going to build it and this is our best option,’ the same way that most people are not happy about their choice of Presidential candidate these days. Many are quite upset that Anthropic turned into another race participant, and then there is a split about whether that still makes Anthropic a good enough least-bad option. I believe, in both cases, that those saying ‘you have to pick one’ are making a mistake, but it is similar. Then there is the larger group of EAs warning that no one can be trusted to build AGI and ASI, period. People are accusing an atheist group of being monotheist because they don’t believe in anyone else’s Gods. I especially don’t appreciate those who accuse EAs and rationalists of being ‘uniquely isolated’ or ‘ideological’ or attached to their beliefs or anything like that, as in: Wes (quote is from Sarah Haider): “They tend to hold very binary understanding of emotions and reason, which are, of course, not actually mutually exclusive” Everyone who views rationalists as caricatures says things like this. Nobody does who has talked to any rationalists for more than 10 minutes. This is the pure form of the Straw Vulcan style of critique that is remarkably common and has little bearing on reality. Another common one, also available within that thread, is ‘if you follow their logic to its conclusion it implies bad things.’ Yes, if you blindly and endlessly extrapolate from chosen beliefs, in a way that approximately zero people actually do, without pausing to realize your mistake, you eventually get to some rather large mistakes. That is true of everyone who believes something, and also is an important hint about difficulties with AI alignment. I do think, similarly to Trace Woodgrains, that EAs in particular will often use calculations to imply things that if fully naively extrapolated would go badly, biting bullets in theory, but then in the face of messy reality they wisely pull back in practice. Sometimes things get taken too far, but if there is not a dramatic penalty for too far and you never take things too far then you are not taking things far enough. Note that I explicitly disendorse the strong form of impartiality, among other related bullets. The classic good faith mistake is to take the ‘in theory’ pronouncements, and then presume people who rhetorically bite those bullets actually fully bite them in practice, or that they would if given the opportunity. Others, such as the Economist profile, talk about EA as having been ‘led astray.’ Usually it is that they abandoned other causes for AI. In the Economist case it is the better critique that they inadvertently sped AI up in various ways, which is highly valid, I was mad about it at the time, but it cannot be undone. The other critique, about becoming a ‘strict-church’ and encouraging earning to give are less clear, and hopefully few people are still doing classic ‘earning to give’ at this point. It got bad enough that Tyler Cowen had to go and write In Defense of Effective Altruism. The defense is measured. EA is endorsed on the margin and as directionally correct. As much as Tyler ‘just says things’ regarding AI existential risk, he agrees that obviously we should pay more attention to AI safety, as well as other EA causes like global poverty. Does Tyler have digs and critiques as well? Why yes he does, but to be directionally right on the margin is high praise from a coauthor of Marginal Revolution. Coefficient Giving’s Alexander Berger responded to Tyler’s defense, while accepting that yes EAs can be arrogant. I will sidestep the AI existential risk rhetoric on both sides, since we’ve heard it all before. I think ‘directionally correct’ is important and spot on. Yes there can be overshooting. I do not, for example and as noted above, endorse impartiality, but most people could be less partial. You don’t want to rely on only doing calculations, but most people desperately need to do more calculations and rely on them more. And so on. The particular failure mode people often highlight is to use utility arguments to plausibly favor some other consideration over humanity, saying that if you multiply, the other consideration is more important. It can be insects or shrimp or what not, or it can in some cases lead to AI successionism, or it can be negative utilitarianism and the focus on suffering to the exclusion of other values. The good news is that all the EAs I know who are actually influential do not make these mistakes where it matters, and I do not think that is a coincidence. I think it is actively a good thing that some people make stupid and stupid looking mistakes like the Shrimp Welfare Project, that then are endlessly mocked, and there is very little call to try and jettison such views or people. You can be wrong. Zac Hill: As someone who’s been pro-EA for a pretty long time, and who appreciates the fundamental philanthropic innovations, I really think “makes consequential choices based on thinking rigorously about doing good” is a strong and emulable trait we could use a lot more of. Any group that collectively takes a handful of big ‘look over here’ shots in the 2010s, where two of them are pandemics and AI, should get you asking what they did right, and yeah maybe let a few of them sound crazy and talk about electron suffering. You don’t have to help fund them. Does EA have an ‘inner ring’? Ozymandias points out that no, you can’t join the secret inner circle of cool effective altruists, because there is no single inner circle, whether or not EAs are cool. There are of course various EAs and rationalists and associated persons with money and power and connections. There is no inner ring. There are only other rings. roon (OpenAI): this is so stupid. there is an inner ring of effective altruists and they are well on their way to being trillionaires, or they’re professors at Oxford, or have a tremendous political lobbying machine Oliver Habryka: Eh, I think this is overstated. The top of the community really is a bunch of people who basically never talk to each other. What’s your guess when Will last talked to Dario last talked to Eliezer last talked to Leopold last talked to Alexander Berger? I think modeling EA as an inner ring doesn’t match how power is actually distributed. Aella: i get the impression there’s a few different inner rings, each with different flavors, and there’s super high variance in communication within and between the rings Anna Salamon: Seconded Oliver Habryka: Yep, this seems right to me. There is an Oxford-EA-ish inner ring. There is somewhat of a rationalist inner ring. There is an Anthropic-adjacent inner ring. There is a Constellation inner ring. And maybe 2-3 more I am forgetting. Walk Away One of the best rationalist norms is that if you are in a conversation, and that conversation is boring to you, or you otherwise want to leave, you can quietly leave. Words cannot express how wonderful this norm is. A lot of why Lighthaven is so wonderful is that within its confines you can use this norm. You are not stuck in a conversation, or in a presentation. There was at least one case during The Curve, despite it being at Lighthaven, where I found myself with someone who I was worried did not understand this, that I did not want to offend, and who kept rejecting my polite bids to wrap up the conversation, and that was super frustrating as the opportunity cost of time was high. The fact that you get in trouble doing this in other cultures only emphasizes this. Rachel: you can tell how rationalist a subculture is based on how socially ok it is to just walk away from things / conversations / talks brooke bowman: God it’s so nice I made a point of being weird like that in other spaces too though bc often ppl just don’t even realize it’s an option Paola: I love that this norm exists. It feels quite liberating, and I practice it relatively regularly when among people who I believe are part of subcultures that allow for it. HOWEVER, I would never in a million years do anything like this (intentionally) among most subcultures. There are many social moves similar to this one that I often watch rationalist-adjacent people make among non-rats (eg, saying “I’m bored, “I don’t want to be spoken to right now”, etc.) and cringe each time I see it happen. For people who want to be taken seriously (or even liked on a basic level) among non-rationalist subcultures, learning how to code switch is one of the most important things you can do. This is especially the case when your standard culture has norms than when applied elsewhere will end up communicating disrespect/disregard for the other party. Yes. You need to be rather confident you can do this within a given space before you do it, especially if you are not especially skilled at doing so. One danger, also often brought up regarding school, is ‘well your life is often going to suck in this way, so we’d better make sure you are prepared by ensuring it sucks now.’ Wes, the Dadliest Catch: This is why I worry about people who pretty much only engage with the rats. The norms are pretty good! But they are very strange and will not work anywhere else Paola: yeah and unfortunately the failure mode is not *just* “people find you weird and unapproachable” but rather “people feel insulted and disrespected.” So yes, you need to emphasize that this is only available within the sacred space. Etiquette norms are now sufficiently fractured, or those with different norms have been sufficiently scattered, that it gets harder to know which norms are in play. Kelsey Piper here analyzes the classic example of attempting to visit a friend in another city and ideally stay with them. Depending on the subculture, the dance and way of communicating the ask, and a possible yes or no, is very different, and there is no ‘safe’ answer except IYKYK. Kelsey Piper: Given our blend of mores, my advice is to reach out to the friend while planning the trip and ask their advice on what neighborhoods to stay in in their city. Then, if they say you can stay with them, say that sounds wonderful but you wouldn’t want to be an inconvenience. Then you’re good, haven’t offended any friends, and are unlikely to have missed out on staying with someone who’d be happy to have you. (In my subculture you can just directly ask. But this is not true in all subcultures). Kelsey’s suggestion is safe in one direction, not putting the other person in a corner or forcing them to turn you down, but it seems risky in terms of potentially missing out. I think you’ll have a substantial number of ball drops at both steps. Guess culture where you have to guess which guess culture leads to a lot of wrong guesses, especially if you’re actually an asker or straight doer and you’re improvising. Or, you could take the approach suggested by Artemis on all this. I don’t advise it. Artemis: most people’s norms are bad and deserve to be disrespected and disregarded michael vassar: This doesn’t get said enough. Trying to avoid accusations of disrespectful treatment of bad norms has already taken us to the brink of the abyss. There’s still hope that we can afford to tolerate tolerance but we absolutely can’t survive by ‘respecting’ symmetry breaking respect Paola: I would hate it if my child grew up thinking these norms were perfectly sane and valid, and I also would want them to know how to navigate them in order to get what they want. items.content: If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? In a documentary premiering Saturday—Super Scam Me—investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure. Sneak peek at National Geographic's Super Scam Me. Scamming a romance scammer Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year. items.title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
items.author: Kate Knibbs, wired.com
items.content: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates. Read full article Comments

items.title: Investors Turn on Data Center Builders as Rising Interest Rates Dampen the AI Trade
items.author: Jonathan Weber
items.content: The Week in Short Rising interest rates are hitting neoclouds hard and threatening AI momentum. Valar Atomics feuds with its own investor, Masha Bucher and Day One. Latest Ramp data shows AI token spend leveling out. Bumble taken private by Ithaca Holdings, a buyout vehicle for top VCs. Ramp and Modal raise big new rounds. Bending Spoons brings in Berkshire Hathaway money, lays off Airtable team. Meta has a big week with Muse models. Ron Conway plays for Team Blue in the midterms. Bloomberg finds a sad story in Marc Andreessen’s hometown. The Main Item CoreWeave & the AI Infrastructure Build-Out Face a Moment of Truth CoreWeave is an archetypal company of the AI boom, for better and for worse. Now the markets are testing its mettle. Launched by a group of finance and bitcoin guys, CoreWeave saw early that there’d be a huge need for AI compute and built a highly leveraged vehicle that deployed massive amounts of capital to serve that need. The risks were obvious from the get-go and CoreWeave’s IPO in the spring of 2025, though rocky out of the gate, had investors quickly send the shares soaring and set the whole neocloud category on fire. Companies including Nebius, Nscale, and Firmus ramped up debt-financed projects backed by Nvidia (both its chips and its equity in some cases) and private credit lenders such as Apollo and Blackstone. Now the grim reaper of rising interest rates, alongside political backlash and general market jitters over the AI trade, is coming for the neoclouds. Anthropic financials that were released this week didn’t provide much comfort. The betting here is that there’s carnage to come. Firmus Grid, an Australian firm, may prove an early indicator. A former Bitcoin miner with close ties to Nvidia and also backed by Coatue, Jane Street, and Blackstone, it tried to go public last week at a valuation of $30 billion, though it only had $59 million in revenue in FY 2026 and has only delivered 46MW of its 912MW data center pipeline. Oh and its CEO had done time for insider trading. That’s circa-2000 bubble vibes for sure. The Firmus IPO was pulled after investors balked at the valuation, and what looked like arrogant overreach, and they ultimately weren’t willing to back it even at a lower price. The company insists it still plans to go public in New York next year and in the meantime will raise private funds, though there’s been no announcement yet. Nscale, which filed to go public last month, has a similar profile: a $35 billion valuation based on contracts with Microsoft and Anthropic, and a big ratio of promised megawatts to actual capacity online. That deal is already looking shaky. CoreWeave, for its part, is battling a bond market that has abruptly become far more skeptical of the AI buildout; its debt was trading at distress levels mid-week before recovering somewhat, but the bonds still pay a 15% yield as of Thursday. Yet the company needs to be able to borrow at investment-grade rates — i.e. more like 6% — for its math to work. Equity investors, still drawn to the upside of the AI trade, are hanging in there; CoreWeave shares have fallen 30% over recent weeks but still sit 60% above its IPO offering price 18 months ago. Yet the company is clearly in the hot seat: CEO Mike Intrator was forced to plead “irrational markets” in explaining the bond selloff, which was amusing given that the whole category is arguably the product of irrational exuberance. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang — deeply invested, both literally and figuratively, in the success of CoreWeave and Firmus — offered a vote of confidence Thursday, insisting that CoreWeave’s cost of capital was actually declining and all would be fine. But a Bloomberg story late in the day showing that CoreWeave founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the IPO isn’t likely to improve the mood of shareholders. Nor did the Anthropic revenues released this week provide a clean narrative for data center bulls. In a meeting for potential public market investors, the company disclosed that it had hit nearly $17 billion in revenue for the third quarter. That’s up 46% from the previous quarter, which is impressive, but well below the explosive 100% growth it showed between the first and second quarters. Around 5% to 7% of Anthropic’s revenue came from “distillation,” a process where rival AI model makers train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones, per the Financial Times. That makes the $2 trillion valuation Anthropic was targeting at its IPO feel like a reach; on Thursday, Reuters reported that some investors were discussing a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. The company is projecting it will spend upwards of $500 billion on data center capacity over the next decade. And cloud providers like Coreweave and the rest are taking on expensive debt in anticipation of Anthropic being able to make good on that projection. It's a risky bet even you believe in AI’s transformative power. Pro Rata Rights Valar Atomics’ Battle with Day One Spotlights the Valley’s Unwritten Rules A key principle of Silicon Valley today is being “founder friendly,” and there are a lot of tacit understandings about what that means. Isaiah Taylor, founder and CEO of Valar Atomics, is trying to enforce the unwritten rules with a lawsuit against his own seed investor, Day One Ventures. When Sequoia invested in the nuclear-reactor maker earlier this year, other investors waived pro-rata rights and “spring back” rights that entitled them to invest more and would have diluted Taylor. But Masha Bucher, Day One’s founder, refused, and after several testy exchanges, Taylor says Bucher called on Quinn Emanuel to send legal threats. You can read Taylor’s version here and Bucher’s response here. Publicly, most people backed Taylor, and some termed the situation “tough”; Silicon Valley founders are untouchable at the moment. But investors we spoke to were privately more sympathetic to Day One’s predicament. The tussle also exposes the Valley’s seesawing founder-investor dynamic. Taylor raised money from Bucher — not a top-tier VC, with ties to suspect Russian investors — when he did not have better options, but after a billion dollars in funding, he felt empowered to rearrange his cap table. Bucher’s side believes she alone was told to give up future pro-rata rights, while other investors were not, according to a source with knowledge. Taylor also gave other investors some allocation, despite their waiving, the person said. These details have not been previously reported. Valar did not respond to a request for comment. “Masha wasn’t some elite VC, but god, what founder will now take money from her after this? How will it look? Can they trust her? And Day One’s name in a press release will now have a wildly different association,” one VC told us. Investors like to say that if like to say if things work as they should, none of the details in complex deal agreements ultimately matter. If Valar becomes a “multi-trillion-dollar company,” as Taylor says it can be, Bucher will make spectacular amounts of money, although the pro-rata might have made the difference between, say, a 100x and a 150x. While the episode in some ways underscores the importance of the fine print, sources told us it was unlikely to spur legal tweaks or challenges at other startups because if VCs over-negotiate, founders will go elsewhere. Newcomer Podcast Alex Kantrowitz on OpenAI, Nvidia & What Could Derail the AI Boom Two Big Charts Enterprise AI Token Spending Levels Out, Ramp Data Shows The growth in new AI customers has dropped significantly, according to fresh business spending data from Ramp. OpenAI managed to narrow Anthropic’s gain and xAI saw a slight uptick due to the popularity of GrokBot, but it wasn’t enough to reverse the trend that began this summer. Meanwhile, AI token spending growth has been basically flat for two months in a row, likely due to price declines at the frontier and the models becoming more efficient overall, writes Ramp chief economist Ara Kharazian. items.title: Meta may use sweeping new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.content: Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts. Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content. As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans. items.title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem. What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world. The Ontology This agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples. api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application . api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" . api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" . INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident . INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway . INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" . In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools. “Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar. We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc. We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores. The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts). Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected. Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain: There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing. The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph. The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples: Creating determinism from non-determinism Building this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time. The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract: # The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates: category IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"] sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"] # Result — a deterministic triple: thread:123 slack:category "incident" . thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean . There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below: The five layers to create determinism from non-determinism Enrichers: Agents as entropy reducers We use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow: class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count) Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers: every entity carries an rdf:type, every URI follows a single naming scheme, and the catalog gates every ops:Application. Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save. This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself. The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chains The correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded. The Correlation Engine The role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them. A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions. The knowledge flywheel Each harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph. The Knowledge Flywheel Observe collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory. Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones. Putting the graph to work On top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this: Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written. Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble. If you want to build one of these A fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt. Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity. Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it. Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve. Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation. Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust. Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed. Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it. Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop. What comes next The graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it. Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge. Acknowledgements None of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix. Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: The new Apple TV 4K just got its first (very small) discount
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.content: The new Apple TV 4K will be available in November. | Image: The Verge Earlier this week, Apple announced its new Apple TV 4K, which costs nearly twice as much as the 2022 model did at launch. Amazon is now offering the first discount on the forthcoming streaming box (coming out on November 13th), just days after discounting Apple’s new smart display for the first time. Right now, you can preorder the latest Apple TV 4K ahead of its November 13th release date for $289.99 ($9 off) at Amazon. Yes, it’s a tiny discount, but every little bit helps given the higher price tag. Apple TV 4K (2026) Where to Buy: $299 $289.99 at Amazon Powered by the new A19 chip, Apple’s latest streaming device now features support for Siri AI out of the box, which is coming to older Apple TV 4K models via a software update. Unlike its predecessors, though, the new model features far-field microphones so you can quickly make hands-free requests. You can, for example, ask for recommendations, like nature documentaries available on Apple TV, or ask questions about what you’re watching. Siri AI can also understand personal context, too, so long as you have an iPhone or iPad connected to your account that supports Apple Intelligence. Apple has made a few other welcome upgrades, though — as my colleague John Higgins points out — not as many as some may have expected. While Apple skipped features we’d hope to see on a $300 streamer, like audio passthrough and support for 120fps output, it’s nice that the Siri Remote now supports Find My precision tracking, so you can make it ring when it goes missing or use the Find My app on your iPhone to pinpoint its location. The new Apple TV 4K also supports a more expansive surround-sound setup, allowing you to pair up to four compatible HomePod speakers instead of just two. Read our hands-on impressions of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Three more Verge-approved deals: If you’ve been meaning to pick up Pikmin 4, Walmart is selling a digital copy for $39.88 ($20 off), which is a great price considering most other retailers are still charging the full $59.99. It’s the original Switch version, but you can upgrade to the forthcoming Nintendo Switch 2 Edition when it arrives on November 12th by purchasing a separate $9.99 upgrade pack, which adds improved graphics and a new Dandori Academy mode. That brings your total to just $49.87, saving you about $20 compared to buying the $69.99 Switch 2 Edition outright. Read our review. All eyes might be on the iPhone Duo — which is now available to preorder, despite shipments being delayed into 2027 — but if you have a non-foldable iPhone, Woot is currently discounting a wide range of Otterbox cases through October 31st. I’ve owned several of the brand’s cases for both my smartphones and tablets over the years, and I’ve been impressed by their durability. I currently use the OtterBox Symmetry Series Clear Case for my iPhone 16, which normally costs $49.99 but is now available in various colors for just $5.99 with a 90-day warranty. The sale also includes cases for other iPhones, as well as some Samsung and Google phones, so it’s worth browsing even if you’re not planning to upgrade your phone anytime soon. Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is on sale for $45.99 ($44 off) at Amazon, which is $5 shy of its best price to date. It’s a handy cordless option for small tasks ranging from tightening screws to assembling desks, with 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling a variety of jobs. The USB-C rechargeable screwdriver also comes with a 220RPM motor and three torque settings, along with a LED light to help illuminate your workspace.
