items.title: Rivian CEO: Robotics Is Progressing Much Faster Than You Think
items.author: Alex Kantrowitz
items.content: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe is behind the wheel of a fully-loaded R1 SUV, plodding through traffic on a dreary Wednesday New York City afternoon, when he tells me people are underestimating the progress in robotics today. “The rate of progress in robotics is going to be far higher than the world knows,” he says. “Far, far, far, far faster.” Scaringe, the 43-year-old CEO of the $18 billion electric car company, founded Mind Robotics, a new robotics company, in 2025, raising $1 billion with a plan to take advantage of the field’s latest advances. The company is building industrial robots that are not quite humanoids, but have two arms, two hands, fingers that splay wider than human digits, and fingernails that can be used to manipulate thin items that require a light touch. Scaringe and I met at Rivian’s showroom on 14th street in New York City this week. And after some schedule jenga, he offered me a ride my podcast studio across town so we could have the maximum amount of time to talk. Expecting a cursory update on a car company, I left with at least some belief that the so-called ‘ChatGPT moment for robotics’ might arrive sooner than anticipated. The key development, Scaringe tells me, is that robots are now starting to learn broad, generalizable skills, unlike their predecessors that moved with prescribed motions, and that is unlocking an array of new possibilities. The transformer model at the heart of LLM technology is also being used to enable these advances as well. “This is a transformer-based model,” Scaringe says. “We’re using transformers to take really complex, diverse sets of data, convert that into models with weights, use those models with weights to drive action.” Instead of telling a robot the exact movements it needs to make to clean a surface, for example, Scaringe says you’re starting to be able to just tell it to clean a surface and its internal model will be able to use generalized motion skills to figure it out. Look at a phone, and it will use its fingers to pick it up. Look at a credit card, and it will use fingernails. Scaringe, who can’t escape being measured up to Elon Musk as a head of an electric car company, is now competing with Musk in robotics as well. Scaringe’s robots are, in a sense, the anti-Optimus. As opposed to Musk’s general purpose humanoids, Scaringe’s bots are factory-centric and meant to be sold to manufacturers. This is because Scaringe belives the economics are better his way. “You need to have a business that’s willing to pay for the robot,” he says. “Would you be willing to pay a robot $10,000 a year to fold your laundry? Maybe, but that’s a small selection. But would you be willing to have a robot that you paid $50,000 a year to work three shifts in a manufacturing plant? Absolutely.” Subscribe now Indeed, Mind Robotics has a deal with Rivian where it trains and runs its latest technology. Within Rivian’s plants, workers wear cameras to feed data about their movements to the robots’ AI models, and they have cameras watching their movements, feeding the data to the models as well. In a sense, it’s modern-day Taylorism, a practice where factory managers watched workers in the industrial age, identified all unnecessary movement, and asked workers to move in regimented motions. This time though, it will be the robots doing the efficient work. Scaringe believes that a wide spectrum of industrial work will be automateable, including an entire factory. “Take a Rivian plant, we have 6,000 robots today, we have 7,000 people,” Scaringe says. “All those jobs that people are doing are things that more advanced robotics could do.” But what of the workers? “I think robotics is going to be like multi-decade transition,” Scaringe says, explaining that the complexity of industrial work will necessitate longer-time-horizon rollouts vs. immediate adoption. Still, he’s under no illusion that the future of human labor will look anything like it does today. “Now it’s pretty rare that you meet a farmer,” he says. “But if this was 125 years ago, that would have been normal. I think the same is going to play out in not just manufacturing, but lots of different segments where the things we’ve done historically are going to start to shift.” Share How $31 Trillion In Datacenters Get Built By 2050 — With Dallas Dolen (sponsor) Dallas Dolen is the TMT leader at PwC. Dolen joins Big Technology to discuss PwC’s projection that global AI infrastructure investment could reach $31 trillion through 2050. Tune in to hear why he believes surging compute demand can outrun efficiency gains, and how the world could generate enough power to support the buildout. We also cover international competition for data centers, growing political opposition, AI’s consumer opportunity, and whether today’s models are already powerful enough to transform business. Hit play for a wide-ranging look at what it will actually take to build the infrastructure behind the AI boom. Watch Here This Week On Big Technology Podcast: The Bumpy Road To AGI — With Kevin Roose Kevin Roose is the author of The AGI Chronicles,. Roose joins Big Technology Podcast to discuss whether an AI industry rife with personal rivalries, infighting, and mistrust can be trusted to develop technology more powerful than humans. Tune in to hear why Roose emerged from years of reporting inside OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind more concerned about AI safety, why he believes the industry should slow down, and what happens if AI systems begin improving themselves. We also cover Sam Altman’s leadership style, Dario Amodei’s motivations, Sergey Brin’s return to Google, Microsoft’s AI missteps, and the behind-the-scenes drama of OpenAI’s boardroom coup. Hit play for an inside look at the personalities, power struggles, and technological breakthroughs shaping the race to superintelligence. items.title: RFK Jr. proposes FDA look the other way on unproven peptides, report says
items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Food and Drug Administration is moving forward with plans to ease access to unproven peptide drugs that are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again movement—despite FDA staff scientists finding that the drugs have not been sufficiently studied to establish safety and efficacy and may cause harms. The FDA submitted an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA "enforcement discretion" on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency. The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the FDA, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica. Read full article Comments

items.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Spending Contracts For Latest AI-Driven Startup Batch
items.author: Joanna Glasner
items.content: Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board. This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here. Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. The biggest round went to AI infrastructure provider Modal Labs, which picked up $750 million, followed by construction automation unicorn Icon, which secured $200 million. Other sectors that attracted larger rounds this past week included biotech, insurance and AI. 1. Modal Labs, $750M, AI infrastructure: Modal Labs, a provider of cloud infrastructure for AI inference and other applications, secured $750 million in a Series D funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation. The New York-headquartered company said it recently exceeded an annual revenue run rate of $1 billion. 2. Icon, $200M, construction tech: Austin-based Icon, a developer of robotic construction systems known for its 3D-printed homes, closed on $200 million in Series D funding led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock. The company says it is on pace for 4x revenue growth in 2026. 3. Soufflé Therapeutics, $135M, RNA therapies: Boston-based Soufflé Therapeutics, a developer of RNA therapies, raised $135 million in Series B funding led by Juvia Group as part of a large syndicate of investors. 4. Estuary Biotherapeutics, $103M, gene therapies: Menlo Park, California-based Estuary Biotherapeutics, a developer of genetic medicines for patients with serious kidney diseases, launched with $103 million in financing. The funding includes $93 million in a Series A round led by RA Capital Management as well as $10 million in previously undisclosed seed capital. 5. Labelbox, $100M, AI tools: Labelbox, a developer of technology to train and evaluate AI models and to help deploy agents that improve with experience, picked up $100 million in Series E funding. Infinitum Partners led the financing for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company. 6. Suki, $90M, health AI: Redwood City, California-based Suki, a provider of AI tools that turn clinical conversations into intelligence for documentation, coding and other healthcare workflows, announced a $90 million Series E financing from backers including Healthier Capital and Crosslink Capital. 7. Abby Care, $82M, caregiver platform: Abby Care, a platform for family members to become certified, paid caregivers and deliver care at home, closed on $82 million in Series C funding, per a Fortune report. Transformation Capital led the financing for the 5-year-old, San Francisco-based startup. 8. Stand, $70M, insurance: Stand, a provider of insurance for homes in areas at higher risk of natural disasters, secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Saga Ventures led the financing for the 3-year-old, San Francisco-based company. 9. Mueon, $65M, semiconductor systems: Mueon Corp., a semiconductor systems company building a modular platform for AI and hyperscale computing, completed a $65 million Series A funding round. Maverick Silicon led the financing for the Portland, Oregon-based company. 10. North.cloud, $60M, AI spend management: New York-based North.cloud, provider of an infrastructure spend intelligence and automation platform, raised $60 million in a Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital. Methodology We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 10-16, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week. Illustration: Dom Guzman
